name: La Bandera
description: Rice, beans, and meat — the national dish of the Dominican Republic, symbolizing unity and tradition.
culturalMeaning: La Bandera represents the Dominican flag, symbolizing unity and national pride through food.
steps: Cook rice until fluffy.
Prepare stewed beans with garlic, onion, and spices.
Season and cook meat (chicken or beef).
Serve rice, beans, and meat together with salad.
funFacts: It is called 'La Bandera' because the colors resemble the Dominican flag.
Most Dominicans eat this dish daily for lunch.

name: Mangú
description: Mashed plantains served with salami, cheese, and eggs, often enjoyed as a hearty breakfast.
culturalMeaning: Mangú is a breakfast staple that reflects African influence and Dominican comfort food traditions.
steps: Boil plantains until soft.
Mash with butter and salt.
Serve with fried salami, cheese, and eggs.
Enjoy hot as a hearty breakfast.
funFacts: Mangú is often called 'Los Tres Golpes' when served with salami, cheese, and eggs.
It is a symbol of Dominican hospitality and family breakfasts.

name: Sancocho
description: A rich stew made with meats, root vegetables, and corn, often prepared for family gatherings and celebrations.
culturalMeaning: Sancocho is a celebratory dish, often cooked for special occasions and family reunions.
steps: Season meats with spices and marinate.
Brown meats, then add water to create broth.
Add root vegetables and plantains.
Simmer until thick and hearty.
Serve hot with rice or avocado.
funFacts: Dominicans often say 'un buen sancocho cura todo' (a good sancocho cures everything).
There are versions with seven meats, considered the most traditional.

name: Tostones
description: Twice-fried plantains, crispy and golden, served as a side dish or snack across the country.
culturalMeaning: Tostones are a versatile snack that highlight the importance of plantains in Dominican cuisine.
steps: Peel and slice plantains.
Fry slices until golden, then flatten.
Fry again until crispy.
Sprinkle with salt and serve with dipping sauce.
funFacts: Tostones are popular across Latin America, but Dominicans often serve them with garlic sauce.
They are a common side dish with fried meats or seafood.
Street vendors frequently sell tostones as a quick snack.

name: Mofongo
description: Mashed fried plantains mixed with garlic, pork cracklings, and broth.
culturalMeaning: Mofongo represents the fusion of African and Caribbean culinary traditions, symbolizing resilience and creativity in Dominican cuisine.
steps: Peel and slice plantains, then fry until golden.
Mash fried plantains with garlic and chicharrón.
Add broth gradually to achieve a soft texture.
Shape into a ball or serve in a bowl.
Top with meat, seafood, or vegetables.
funFacts: Mofongo is also popular in Puerto Rico, but the Dominican version often uses more broth.
It is considered a comfort food and is commonly served with chicken or shrimp.

name: Pastelón
description: A layered casserole of sweet plantains, ground beef, and cheese.
culturalMeaning: Pastelón is often called the Dominican lasagna, showcasing the blend of local ingredients with European influences.
steps: Peel and slice ripe plantains, fry until golden.
Cook ground beef with onions, peppers, garlic, and tomato sauce.
Layer fried plantains, beef mixture, and cheese in a baking dish.
Pour beaten eggs over the layers to bind.
Bake until golden and set.
funFacts: Pastelón is a festive dish often served at family gatherings and holidays.
Its sweet‑savory flavor makes it unique compared to Italian lasagna.

name: Habichuelas con Dulce
description: A sweet bean dessert made with red beans, coconut milk, and spices.
culturalMeaning: This dessert is a symbol of Dominican Easter traditions, shared among families and neighbors during Holy Week.
steps: Boil red beans until soft, then blend into a smooth puree.
Cook beans with coconut milk, evaporated milk, sugar, and spices.
Add raisins and sweet potato chunks.
Simmer until thick and creamy.
Serve chilled, often with cookies or crackers.
funFacts: Habichuelas con Dulce is unique to the Dominican Republic — few countries turn beans into dessert.
It is so popular during Easter that supermarkets stock special kits with all ingredients.

name: Locrio
description: A flavorful rice dish cooked with seasoned meat, vegetables, and spices, often compared to paella.
culturalMeaning: Locrio is a staple of Dominican home cooking, symbolizing practicality and flavor in everyday meals.
steps: Season meat with garlic, salt, pepper, and spices.
Brown meat in oil, then add onions, peppers, and tomato paste.
Add rice and stir to coat with seasonings.
Pour in water or broth, cover, and cook until rice is tender.
Fluff rice and garnish with cilantro before serving.
funFacts: Locrio is considered the Dominican version of paella, but simpler and more rustic.
It’s a versatile dish — families prepare it with chicken, pork, or even sardines depending on availability.
